extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers learning/working in enumerative combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes a satisfactory determination of a counting function and how to prove/evaluate counting results (closed forms, recurrences, algorithms, estimates, generating functions, and combinatorial proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed formula (explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most satisfactory form of f(i) is a completely explicit closed formula involving only well-known functions, and free from summation symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only in rare cases will such a formula exist. As formulas become more complicated, willingness to accept them as satisfactory decreases. Example: f(n)=2^n is ideal; more complicated sums (even if explicit) are less elegant. Beware formulas that are "non-combinatorial" (e.g., dividing by e and rounding) since they lack direct combinatorial significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Give f(i) by a recurrence in terms of previously calculated f(j)'s, thereby providing a simple procedure to compute f(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurrences are acceptable when they yield simple computation (example: Fibonacci-type recurrences). Pay attention to indexing choices — choosing convenient indexing can make conversion to generating functions and solution simpler. Recurrences can be the basis to obtain generating functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an algorithm to compute f(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An algorithmic determination subsumes closed forms and recurrences; acceptability depends on elegance and performance. Prefer algorithms whose running time is substantially less than f(i) itself; otherwise it's effectively brute-force listing of objects and not useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate / asymptotic formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an estimate g(n) for f(n), typically in the asymptotic sense f(n) ~ g(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asymptotic estimates are often superior to complicated explicit formulas for understanding growth; standard asymptotic notation and analytic techniques can be used to derive and justify these estimates (example: nearest integer to n!/e or Stirling-like asymptotics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating function representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent f(n) by a generating function (ordinary or exponential formal power series); this is the most useful but most difficult method for evaluating f(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat generating functions as formal power series in C[[x]] (or multivariate). Algebraic operations (addition, multiplication, composition, inversion, exponentiation, differentiation) have combinatorial meaning and can be used to extract recurrences, explicit formulas, and asymptotic estimates. Composition is well-defined when the inner series has zero constant term; inversion requires nonzero constant term. Use formal convergence (stabilization of coefficients) to justify infinite sums/products. Examples: differentiate to get recurrences; expand exponentials to get explicit coefficient formulas; use analytic methods for asymptotics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial meaning of formula terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer formulas whose terms have clear combinatorial interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formula is more acceptable if every term has an easily understood combinatorial meaning (example: terms arising from Inclusion–Exclusion). A formula that is algebraically explicit but lacks combinatorial interpretation (e.g., round(n!/e)) is less satisfactory for combinatorial understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and elegance criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity and elegance of the form in which f is presented affect acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a complicated explicit formula is correct, simpler expressions are preferred; as complexity increases, willingness to accept decreases. The form should balance explicitness with interpretability and computational practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: formulas requiring listing objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'formula' whose evaluation requires listing all (or almost all) of the f(n) objects being counted is worthless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid definitions or representations that give no computational or conceptual advantage over brute-force enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for bijective (combinatorial) proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving that two finite sets have the same cardinality, prefer exhibiting an explicit one-to-one correspondence (bijection) between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combinatorial (bijective) proof is generally better than a non-combinatorial counting proof because it gives insight and often a shorter argument. Constructive bijections should avoid circular reasoning (do not use the equality of cardinalities to argue bijectivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal power series calculus and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When using generating functions, treat them as formal power series and use the formal calculus (algebra, derivation, exponentiation) that applies in C[[x]] and C[[x1,...,xm]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic laws (associativity, commutativity, distributivity) hold; inversion exists iff constant term nonzero; differentiation and composition rules apply (composition requires inner series constant term 0). Exponentiation (1+F)^λ can be defined formally for F(0)=0; log and exp manipulations valid when interpreted formally. Use formal convergence notion: coefficient stabilization or degree growth for infinite sums/products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generating functions to extract different types of information
rubrics_metrics.description: From a generating function one should extract recurrences, explicit coefficient formulas, and asymptotic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show differentiation of generating function gives recurrences; product/expansions give explicit coefficient summations; analytic properties as complex functions let one apply asymptotic methods to estimate coefficients. Present generating functions when they concisely encode multiple useful properties of the counting sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and presentation choices matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of indexing or how a recurrence is written can greatly simplify subsequent manipulations (e.g., conversion to generating functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-index recurrences or shift indices to obtain simpler generating-function identities or differential equations. Small changes in indexing can make derivations much more tractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify formal manipulations (algebraic vs analytic viewpoints)
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating formal power series, justify formal identities either algebraically (polynomial identities, coefficient stabilization) or via function-theoretic arguments when series converge in a neighborhood of 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that formal identities follow from analytic identities when applicable (agree on neighborhood of 0) or prove coefficient-wise equalities by finite-polynomial dependence. Use continuity/density arguments (polynomials dense in formal series) when needed to extend identities formally.
